p.t: In short
p.s: Use mentors, coaches, masterminds and peers

p.t:
Ask a mentor **specific, deep questions** only. Search the basics yourself first.
Pick **one strategy** and follow it. Stop comparing many methods.

Before each paid call, **book, fill in the survey, then email your topics**.
If you are stuck, **ask for help early**. Do not lose days on one task.
Use only the **official support email** or community. Ignore strangers who offer private help.

Join a **mastermind**, a small group of 3 to 5 peers who help each other reach goals.
Meet on a **fixed schedule**, such as every two weeks, or the group falls apart.

Pick peers at **about the same stage** of building their business.
**Give help first**, because help comes back to you.
Choosing a mentor and a single strategy
p.s: Use mentors, coaches, masterminds and peers

p.t: Pay for mentorship (paid guidance from an experienced person) only when you can ask **specific, in-depth** questions.
Generic questions that a quick web search can answer waste the investment.
Focus mentorship questions on what cannot be found by a basic search, because a mentor can share knowledge that is not easily found online.

Pick **a single strategy** (one plan for how you run the business) from one mentor and follow it. Do not second-guess among many approaches. This reduces decision fatigue (feeling worn out from too many choices).
Learn the basics on your own before getting mentorship. Use the mentor to **speed up** progress, not to replace learning.
Mentorship from an experienced coach is a practical investment for a beginner.
It shortens the path through product research (finding products worth selling), ad testing (trying ads to see what works) and payments (setting up how customers pay).
Compared with self-funded trial and error (learning by paying for your own mistakes), a coach shortens that path.
A beginner with no experienced person to ask tends to repeat avoidable mistakes and lose money on them.
Active community channels (chat rooms inside a community) where experienced operators answer questions and give feedback **shorten that learning curve**.
Mentorship gives an exponential advantage (a benefit that grows faster and faster over time).
Successful people usually had a mentor. A mentor helps you avoid repeating known mistakes.
Free YouTube content is enough to learn ads fundamentals (the basics of ads) and how to read ad logic.
Add a mentor or consultation when you hit a specific problem, such as not knowing why ads fail after a first campaign.
Keep improving and keep working after the mentorship ends. Success often comes **months** after the programme.

Results come from steady daily work rather than the course itself.
The paid mentoring period lasts **three months**.
Within those three months, a beginner should be able to build the store, launch ads and start making sales.
If the student is not yet confident running Facebook ads (paid adverts on Facebook) at the end, support continues until they are.

In a mentorship program, you choose **which mentor to book** for each call.
You can book several calls with the same mentor or with different mentors.
Preparing questions and surveys
p.s: Use mentors, coaches, masterminds and peers

p.t: Write the questions down **before each call** so you can check during the session that every topic you need is covered.
Making notes is the **minimum requirement** even if you are unsure there will be enough time.
Ask questions that solve a real problem you cannot work out yourself.
Do not ask for things you can look up. Better questions speed up progress more than waiting for answers.
If you are unsure whether you are reasoning about a niche (a narrow group of buyers with one shared need) or product correctly, **ask a coach** on a group or one-to-one call.
Bring the specific criteria you are unsure about so the coach can check them.
If you feel stuck during market selection (choosing which market to sell to), **ask for help** instead of letting the same doubts loop in your head.
Asking questions is a normal and expected part of building a business.
Once you have a shortlisted niche (a niche you narrowed down to), **get a second opinion** from a coach, a team review, or a market verification check (a check that real buyers exist).

Outside input helps you test how you are thinking about the market.
Asking questions in a community is a good way to get **a single stuck step** solved.

Rephrase the question and ask again later if it goes unanswered.
Pre-coaching survey (a short form to fill in before coaching), in order:

1. Find the survey link in the resources section, or use the copy sent by email.
2. Open the link in a web browser.

3. Answer the questions one by one.
4. Click submit.
5. A confirmation message appears, and the answers are sent automatically to the coaching team. No further action is needed after that.
Complete the pre-coaching survey **before the first coaching call**.
The coaching team uses the answers to learn about the person and business and to review the website in advance.
The survey asks basic questions about the person and the business.
Coaching calls should not be spent on basic background questions, so the survey handles that information before the call.

Each coaching session is **one hour**, so preparing in advance lets the time go straight to useful help.
A single coaching session lasts **one hour**.
Preparing for paid one-to-one sessions
p.s: Use mentors, coaches, masterminds and peers

p.t: Paid one-to-one sessions (private sessions with one coach) **only pay off when you plan before the call**.
Without a plan, the session is spent finding data and deciding what to discuss instead of solving problems.
Do not book a one-to-one session **without a clear topic and a defined outcome** you want to achieve.
Booking a call just to have a chat gives uncertain value for the money paid.
Before each call, the basic pre-consultation survey (a short form before the call) must be completed **after booking**.

Preparation for every upcoming call follows the same sequence: **book, complete the survey, then email the topics and details.**
Procedure for preparing a one-to-one coaching session:

1. Book the call.
2. Complete the pre-consultation survey.
3. Decide exactly which topics you want to cover, which questions you want to ask, and what you need help with.
4. Write the questions down as notes on paper, a computer or a phone so you can refer to them during the call.
5. Decide which supporting information the reviewer (the coach who checks your work) cannot already see. Use your own judgment and do not worry about getting it perfect.
6. Add links to specific website sections you want to discuss.

7. Grant access to Google Analytics (a free tool that shows who visits your website) and Google Ads (Google's paid ad service) **if paid traffic data** (data on visitors who come through paid ads) must be reviewed.
8. Copy the emails you want reviewed, or paste their body text.
9. Send **one email** to the support address listed in the course resources before each call. It should contain the list of topics and questions plus any attachments or links.
10. If you are unsure what material is needed or lack time, send at least the list of topics and questions.
11. If the reviewer replies asking for specific material, provide it before the call.
Preparing for paid one-to-one sessions (continued)
p.s: Use mentors, coaches, masterminds and peers

p.t: Before each call, **email the support address** listed in the course resources with your list of topics, questions, and any attachments or links.

This is best practice and should take little time.
If you lack time or are unsure what material is needed, send at least the list of topics and questions.

The reviewer may reply asking for specific material before the call.
Sending material in advance lets the reviewer read it before the call.
Session time is then used for discussion and advice rather than silent reading. Only material the reviewer cannot already access needs to be sent.

If there is more to cover than fits in one session, **handle the leftover topics after the call**.
Do not let fear of running out of time stop you from preparing.
Every member has an onboarding call (a welcome call with the program host or a team member), booked through a link sent by email.
The call clarifies your stage and which content to prioritise, so **book it before starting the course**.
If you get stuck, use the support available, such as scheduled support calls, Q&A sessions (question and answer sessions),

the community chat and mentors.
Use that support **before deciding to quit**. Ask for help on the specific step you cannot complete.

If a task planned for 30 to 60 minutes takes about **two hours** and you are stuck, stop trying alone and ask for help.
Do not let days go by on one task.

If you are unsure whether you are progressing well, talk to an experienced person who can review your situation.
Do not judge yourself against public success posts.
A personal coach should be consulted **every week or every two weeks**, or at least monthly, to report progress.
The coach should ask questions that help you find your own solutions rather than giving direct advice.
Peer communities (groups of other business owners) such as fastbusinessforum.com and the Source A Labs Facebook group are used to ask questions and get answers from operators in many markets

and circumstances.
Post a specific question there to get **on-the-ground answers** when stuck.
Ongoing questions go to the members-only Facebook group.

2. If nothing relevant exists, post the question in the group.
3. Ask questions about one specific topic in the comments under the matching topic, where the answer is visible to everyone reading that topic.
4. For account or access problems and anything not answered elsewhere, email the support address listed in the course resources.
5. For personal help, book group coaching calls or a paid one-to-one coaching session.
Attend the scheduled coaching calls, since they are **one of the main support resources** alongside the private Facebook group.

Use them to get help as you work through the build steps.

p.t:
Hosts can be contacted directly through a Facebook friend request.
Messenger (Facebook's chat app) is usually open for short questions.
Use these channels **only for genuine questions** about the business or program, never to offer services or sell to other members.
When Google Ads results stall (when ads stop producing results), ask people who run the same type of business and already get better ad results.
You can also post the question in a community of operators in your niche.
Peers with similar stores can often point to the specific setting or page problem behind the issue.
Students should expect to **test a product** with a support ticket (a request sent through the help system) and a store review (a check of the store by a coach) before spending on ads.
The program is built around getting someone to check each step rather than guessing alone.
Common early pain points are an unclear product choice, a store that looks finished but does not sell, and not knowing what went wrong after a failed ad test.
Source D community channels **#resources and #tools** (chat rooms named resources and tools) are the first stop.
Join the community, go through those channels, introduce yourself, and register for the weekly live calls.
Community calls and channels are the fastest path to answers if you get stuck during the first week.
Official communication runs **only through the community's ticket system** (a request form for help).
Ignore direct messages (private messages) from anyone claiming to be training staff who offer personal help with the course.

Treat unsolicited private messages as suspicious.
Ask questions in a community to get **a single stuck step** solved.
Rephrasing and asking again later is acceptable.
Community rules and conduct
p.s: Use mentors, coaches, masterminds and peers

p.t: The community must stay respectful.
Avoid comments that an average person or the law would consider inappropriate, and avoid topics such as politics and religion, because the space is meant for building businesses.

Breaking any of the **four core rules** can lead to immediate removal from the program.
Removal comes with **no refund and no prior warning**.
The four core rules cover inappropriate conduct, selling services to members, direct messages for sales, and sharing content.

The refund exclusion is part of the terms accepted at sign-up.
Sharing wins in the group is encouraged, because entrepreneurs often work alone and feel isolated.

Celebrate milestones such as building a first website, making a first sale, or reaching a thousandth sale, and support others who are struggling.
Asking questions is expected.

A question that feels basic is still better than getting stuck.
Being active, including joining calls even as a listener, tends to increase results in the program.
Questions asked in the comments under a topic notify the person who asked when a team member or another member replies.
The question and answer stay visible to everyone reading that topic, so **the same question does not need to be asked twice**.
Searching before posting avoids duplicate questions (the same question asked twice) and saves waiting time.
Asking in the group or topic comments benefits everyone, because other members with the same problem can read the answer later.

Check the community's announcements channel **regularly**.
Updates are posted almost every day, not only before live calls.

Missing an announcement can mean missing a call or a change to the schedule.
Group coaching is included in the standard membership with **unlimited access**.
It is found in the learning dashboard menu (the member home page for the program) under a group coaching link. It shows the schedule for the current calendar month.
To join the members-only Facebook group, open the group link from the resources section, and request to join.

Access is granted shortly after the request is reviewed.

A notification email is sent when the new schedule is up.
Group coaching calls are split by business stage. One set is for people still building their first business, and another set is for the growth phase after launch.

Choose the calls that match the stage you are in.

Coaching recordings are useful for catching up on past calls.
They often contain practical insight beyond the core course material, so they build a library members can revisit.

Mastermind setup
p.s: Use mentors, coaches, masterminds and peers

p.t: Small peer groups called **masterminds** (groups of peers who meet regularly to help each other) keep members accountable (answerable to

others for their goals).
Committing to tasks before a recurring call (a meeting that repeats on a set schedule) makes people more likely to finish them.

Look in community channels (online groups or forums where members talk) for people on a similar timeline.
Agree on a **fixed call schedule** with them.
Stay connected with other business owners. Use masterminds, community groups or small peer calls.

This keeps your momentum (steady forward progress) going.
If no mastermind exists, **start one** or post in the community.

To find a mastermind, **search the community forum** (the online discussion board) for "mastermind."
Join any that fit.

If none exist, post an introduction.
In it, state your **stage** (the point you have reached in the program) and that you want to start one.

Masterminds work best when members are at **about the same stage**.
Sharing your current progress makes matching easier.
A mastermind gives a **home-based operator** (someone who runs a business from home) the social contact an office job would otherwise provide.
**Synergy** (a group doing better together than each member would alone) means the group's combined progress beats what each member would reach alone.

Peers who hit their targets motivate the others.
Members hold each other to their goals.
Masterminds need a **fixed schedule** to stay active.

Without a set schedule and responsibility, the group dissolves (falls apart).
Mastermind format, standard procedure:

1. Fix a recurring call **every two weeks** at the same time.
2. Give each member **10 to 15 minutes** to speak.
3. Assign **one person** to take notes.
Mastermind setup (continued)
p.s: Use mentors, coaches, masterminds and peers

p.t: 4. At the next meeting, **review the previous notes**, check where each member stands, and touch base (check in briefly) on progress.

Three questions to structure each mastermind session:
1. **What are you working on right now?** Others may learn from it or find a faster method.
2. What do you need help with? Members can ask peers privately instead of posting in public forums.
3. What can you share that will help everyone else? This forces each member to contribute and creates the synergy effect.

Join or start a small recurring group call with **about five peers** in the same field.
In these calls, members share mistakes and wins openly.
Learning from the group's shared mistakes shortens the **learning curve** (the time it takes to become skilled).
This also reduces isolation (feeling alone) in the early stage.
Share **what worked and what did not** over the past month with a peer group of established store owners (people who already run a shop).

Sharing builds familiarity. It tends to draw out others' experiences in return.
Post an open question with your own results first. This makes it easier for others to respond.
A peer community, such as a Discord group (a chat app with topic channels), is useful for sharing problems.
Being heard helps even when no one can solve the problem, because it **reduces stress**.
Active members, mentors (experienced guides) and students alike often offer solutions.

p.s: Use mentors, coaches, masterminds and peers

p.t:
Keep a mastermind at **three to five members**.
Two members is just catching up with a friend.

More than five makes the group too diluted (thinned out) to be personal.
Mastermind size and **cadence** (how often it meets) differ between sources:

Size: 3 to 5 members

Choose mastermind partners at a **similar business stage**.
A person still selecting a **niche** (a narrow market to sell to) should not be grouped with someone already running a large operation.

Peers at the same level benefit most.
Build a network of peers at the same stage by **telling people where you stand**.

Look for others in the same process.
Members should click personally (get along well).
Members should share similar values and similar goals.

Members should feel comfortable sharing business details.
This makes collaboration much easier than it is with people at a different level.

Mastermind members do not have to share their niche with every member.
**Build friendships first.**
Then work most closely with the people whose progress and feedback help you most.

Joining or starting a mastermind of **about 3 to 5 members** that meets weekly helps you stay on track after a pause.
Each member shares struggles and the others support them.
Confidentiality and trust
p.s: Use mentors, coaches, masterminds and peers

p.t: Protect **confidentiality (keeping things private) by signing a one-page agreement**.
In it, every member promises not to share what is discussed with anyone outside the group.
Keep the talks light and useful rather than social chat, so members look forward to each session.
Peer examples in person help make an ambitious goal feel achievable.
Conferences, meetups (local get-togethers), and casual talks with people running similar businesses shift what a person believes is possible.
**Operators** (people who run a business) working in different countries and markets can give market-specific answers that a single-region view cannot.
Forming masterminds and connecting with peers are ways to keep learning and growing a business.
To find a business partner or mastermind partner, **post a short introduction** in an online community.
The introduction states who you are, where you are, what you are looking for, and what kind of partner you want.

**Celebrating peers' wins** raises your own energy and motivation.
Seeing a peer succeed shows that a goal is reachable.

Seeing others succeed also pushes you to work harder.
Accountability works better when goals are **told to peers**, because unmet goals alone are easy to dismiss.

Small stakes or wagers (small bets) within the group can make goal tracking fun.
They also increase follow-through (finishing what you start).
Joining a network of entrepreneurs speeds up learning, because peers share mistakes and resources.
**Reciprocity** (giving and getting back) is required so that value flows both ways.
Networking and partner outreach
p.s: Use mentors, coaches, masterminds and peers

p.t: **Build relationships before you urgently need** traffic (visitors to your shop) or sales.

The work only pays off when it has already been done.
Starting late is like digging a water source only after you are already in need.
Relationship building produces **compounding results** (results that grow on top of earlier ones) with consistency.

The more regular effort you invest, the stronger the outcomes.
**Sporadic** (irregular) effort yields weaker results.
Introverts (quiet people who prefer to work alone) or people who find this outreach daunting (scary or overwhelming) can still succeed through **small, consistent steps**.
Results usually turn out better than expected once action is taken.
Do the well-digging activity **consistently**. Well-digging means slow, steady groundwork done before you need it.

Do not worry about how long it will take.
**Spend a little time each day.**
Expect many days to have little to do, because most **prospects** (people or businesses you hope to work with) publish only occasionally.
Do not interact with a **Dream 100 prospect** without a reason. A Dream 100 list is a list of 100 people or businesses you want to connect with.
Only comment when they have published something new, such as a weekly blog post or a YouTube video published once a week.

This keeps the process manageable and avoids **spamming** (sending too many unwanted messages).
A Dream 100 list does not have to reach exactly 100 names.

The goal is to get as far as you can.
It can be built gradually in small daily sessions alongside other tasks.
Daily action for this stage: **work through the whole Dream 100 list**.

p.t:
Follow, subscribe, like, join groups and forums, create forum accounts, and subscribe to email lists for each contact.
Partnership action plan:
1. Keep engaging with each Dream 100 prospect's content.
2. Once you reach **about 10 touch points** (contacts or interactions), or about 5 for periodic publishers (people who post on a regular schedule), reach out directly.

3. Set up calls and have conversations as your time allows.
4. Book any advertising opportunities you uncover that your budget can afford.
5. Repeat this over the coming months.

Build a **supportive network** that holds you accountable.
Be valuable to others, and reciprocity returns.

Leverage (use) mentorship and community, because you are social by nature.
Build a network of people you both add value to and learn from.

Share mistakes and wins within the group so everyone grows faster.
**Give value first** without expecting a direct return.

Use the network for accountability by **publicly committing to goals**.
Reciprocity is required so that value flows both ways in any entrepreneur network.
Set **a concrete implementation goal** (a specific task to carry out) between coaching calls (sessions with a coach).

Review progress at the next session.
Committing to tasks before a recurring call makes people more likely to complete them.

So **agree on a fixed call schedule** with peers.
If you are unsure whether you are progressing well, talk to an experienced person who can review your situation.
A regular fixed call time with a mentor or accountability coach keeps students on track better than **ad hoc** (unplanned) calls that get cancelled at short

notice.
Reliable schedules also protect the mentor's credibility (how much others trust them).
